utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. May we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, my name is Niemann. I appear with my colleagues Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Ms. Udo for the Prosecution, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Mr. Delalic is also represented by my colleague Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, a professor from Canada. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Zelko Olujic, attorney from Croatia, Defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic, along with my colleague Tomislav Kuzmanovic, attorney from the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo along with Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas. We represent Mr. Hazim Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm Cynthia McMurrey, and along with my colleague Ms. Nancy Boler, we represent Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly bring in the witness. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please remind him he's still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, please. RUSMIR SAFET HADZIHUSEINOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, I just want to start off this morning by showing you a couple of documents and asking you whether or not it's your signature that's on the bottom of them. I don't need you to go into any explanation. It's just a question of saying yes or no, it isn't so. Perhaps, the first one I would ask you to look at is Exhibit P-144 VA-6. Would you have a look at that for me, please? There's a number of documents that appear there. While you're looking at that one, perhaps Madam Registrar may get out the other document for me which is Exhibit D-144 V-A/25. Doctor, the documents that you've now been show, P-144, there's a bundle of documents there. Firstly, one is a covering letter, if I might call it that; secondly, the minutes of a meeting or a decision. Do you see at the foot of both of those documents a seal and a signature that appears there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you able to confirm whether or not that is your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are these documents familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What are these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They are documents that were tendered in support of the expert witness but were admitted for limited purposes only, Your Honour, in support of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But what do they show?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just give a short description.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. These are documents relating to decisions of the war presidency and relate to, in particular, the appointment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes, I recall, but you ask him under what circumstances he made these appointments, because his position has been throughout that the war presidency had nothing to do with the defence organisation of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I'll come to that, Your Honours. I merely just wish to tender them at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The second document that you were shown, Doctor, that's D-144 V-A/25. That's an authorisation, is it not? Do you see the signature and seal that appears at the bottom of that document? For Your Honours benefit --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is rather illegible, I mean, the copy is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, it is a bad copy. I'm just asking you if you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, relying upon the English version that I've been provided, again, it's a Defence document provided in support, this relates to an authorisation for the supply of uniforms and other military means and equipment. I tender those documents, if Your Honours please, for the truth of their contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, yesterday in the course of my cross-examination, I asked you about the issue of the supply of military equipment that was engaged in by the -- well, I think I may have misspoke indeed about the war presidency in the early part of the war. The document I had in mind, but couldn't find at the time, was Exhibit P-66, and I'd just ask you to look at that document, in order to correct any error that I may have made. I note that it's a document of the 12th of April, 1992 and is, in fact, the crisis staff of the assembly. That document also bears your signature, I think, does it, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I know it relates to an earlier period of time than the war presidency, but it concerns itself with the supply of equipment, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Now, in relation to the crisis staff, Doctor, when was the crisis staff first established in the Konjic municipality; can you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yesterday, I think I clarified it amply. Even before the war, that is, during the peace time, there were bodies which were to have been appointed in the extraordinary circumstances, and the extraordinary circumstances could be a large disasters, immediate threat of war and these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's not go into the history of how it could be appointed. When was the crisis staff appointed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The crisis staff was established immediately after the immediate threat of war was declared, and its establishment was provided for not only in Konjic but in all municipalities in such cases. This would have been the crisis staff and the council for people's defence. I think I clarified that yesterday and they functioned until 17 April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We didn't want the history of how it was established.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that I have stated all this very clearly yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This exhibit, and perhaps you might put the English version on the overhead projector for their Honours to see. In this exhibit that you have in front of you, Exhibit 66, it says on the second page, particularly, Mr. Usher, you might put the second page on after showing the first page; it makes reference to you liaising with the Grude headquarters. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I had stated clearly that one of the components of the defence forces of Konjic was the HVO. The Croatian Defence Council had its own superior command, and this command in terms of issuing commands, orders, was in Grude and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with that document, thank you, Doctor. Yesterday we had some discussion about the question of orders, and I showed you one document in relation to orders being issued by the war presidency. I think that you made some distinction about those matters, but I'd now ask you to look at a number of documents that were supplied by the Defence in this case. The first one is Exhibit D-144 V-A/12. Again, Your Honours, for your benefit, this is an order by -- purports to be an order by the president of the presidency relating to civil defence and staff economy, in relation to the necessary number of blankets for persons detained in Celebici prison. Now, do you notice that that document is headed "Order"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I ask you to look at another document, if you would for me, and that is Exhibit D-144/V-A13.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, do you see that document and this, again, Your Honours, is a decision of the war presidency purported to be signed by the witness, and it relates --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: -- to the health centre. Do you notice that that is headed "Decision"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, that's your signature and seal that appears at the foot of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would you look at the next document that I show you? That's Exhibit D-144 V-A-14. This relates to the confiscation of registration plates of vehicles, which are to be placed at the disposal of the war presidency, should they be confiscated; is that right? It's an order that has got headed "Order"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, that bears your signature, does it not, and the seal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It's sent to the police station but, secondly, to the command, submitted to secondly -- the first reference is to the police station and then the command. You have to say "yes," Doctor, otherwise it can't be taken down in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would like you to look at another document which is D-144 V-A/15. Again, this is a document headed "Order" and it provides that all members of the defence forces of Konjic TO and HVO are forbidden to use vehicles, a particular type of vehicles. Doctor, that again bears your signature, does it not, and your seal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, that is sent to the Electra Herzegovina Company and then secondly to the command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, finally, would you look at the next document which is shown to you, which is D-144 V-A/16. This is again an order and, I think, signed by yourself with your seal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Its address provides that the military staff of the defence forces of the Konjic municipality is obliged to ensure unique consumption of crude oil, et cetera. I don't need to go into details. Again, that's submitted to the command. Doctor, looking at all these documents that I've now shown you, isn't it a fact that when you are issuing directives, as it were, to civilian bodies, such as is shown in the second document that you looked at, I think it was the second document, the document D-144 V-A/13, it's interesting, is it not, that the places to whom it is directed are all civilian bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But when a document is headed "Order," at least one of the bodies that it is directed to is the military command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that there is a distinction between directions and decisions -- I should say "decisions." There's a distinction between decisions and orders, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only in terms of the words themselves, not in terms of the essence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I'm finished with those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender them all, Your Honour. The doctor has identified the signature and seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, I understand that yesterday in your evidence in chief, you testified that it was quite clear what were the competencies of the various entities in the Konjic municipality at the relevant time during 1992; did you say something or something to that effect yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was the competent entity for the Celebici prison during the period May to November of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It certainly was not the war presidency or any of the bodies appointed by it. As far as the competencies for prisons are concerned, even before the war and during the war, it was only the police bodies and the investigating bodies that could have that and not civilian ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned in your evidence an occasion when some Arab journalists wanted to visit the Celebici prison and other facilities; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was that a request only made on one occasion or was there more than one occasion when Arab journalists wanted to visit Celebici, that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, and yesterday I think I was very clear, I remember that this group of journalists stayed in my mind very vividly because -- let me repeat this -- they not only wanted to talk to me in my office, but they also wanted to visit the front lines and the prison in Celebici. And then this is why I recall it so vividly. But, there were many visits of Croatian journalists to Konjic as I said yesterday, but this one stayed in my mind because this group of journalists wanted to visit the front lines, which was very dangerous, as well as the prison at Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when they came, you, I think, it's your evidence that you approached the TO for their authority for them to, for these journalists, Arab journalists, to visit the prison, was that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. I said that they came unannounced to the war presidency and that they requested what I have just said. And among other things, we talked about Konjic, about the living conditions there and, in addition to that, they asked for these two things. And since I was not competent for either of these two things which they requested, I directed them to the bodies which were competent for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, what was the body competent for Celebici that you directed them to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is what I said a minute ago. These were the competent police and military investigating bodies. It was not in my authority as part of the body which I represented, so I was not -- I had no interest in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Didn't you say yesterday that you directed them to the TO? You didn't mention anything about the police. You said they were directed to the TO. That was your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I directed them to the structures who potentially could help them to fulfil this wish of theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, I put it to you that you said yesterday that you only mentioned that you directed them to the TO, and you only mentioned the TO, and that was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If this is what you say and if this is what has been taken down, I have nothing against that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, at least, at that stage, you must have thought that the TO had authority over Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not Territorial Defence, as a territorial defence, but a body of it may be a military investigating body or a police body because those are the bodies who should control this, rather than civilian ones. And I believe this is all very clear. There's nothing unclear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now I think you also testified in the course of your evidence-in-chief, that the war presidency had no authority to appoint members to the military investigative committee or to give them any assignments, was that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They could not do that. When you're referring to that, I just wanted a clarification. When you're referring to the military investigative committee in relation to Celebici, or were you making some sort of general comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure I understand what you're -- what you're asking me. I don't know about this military investigative commission, I believe that it is clear what body this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And it's something that the war presidency had nothing to do with, is that a fair statement? If it's not, please correct me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely. It never appointed such a commission, nor did it have any competencies in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at Exhibit P-125 for me please. May I see that document? I am not sure that it's the one I am referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This document probably referred to the commission for finding out the persons killed or persons --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It's not the document I am referring to, Your Honour. Is that P-125?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's Document 125, Prosecutor document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'll come back to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, excuse me a moment, there seems to be some confusion with the documents, so I'll come back to it. So if you'll just put that aside for now, thank you. Doctor, during the course of 1992, did you ever have any contact or receive any reports from Mr. Pavo Mucic about the Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with him at all, that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I saw Pavo Mucic only once and he was wearing civilian clothes and he was in the Celebici barracks compound and he had some kind of a car there, I think it had foreign registration plates and he used it. On the second occasion, when I saw him, was when I visited this complex during the swearing in ceremony and I remember well that he had a camera at that time and he was taping something. So, these were the only occasions on which I ever saw or had any contact with this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, if Mr. Mucic had said to an investigator from the Tribunal that, that before and after he was appointed camp commander, he always tried to keep -- to help them, always informed the town headquarters, the chief, the Mayor of Konjic, Rusmir Hadzihuseinovic, and Zejnil Delalic; you would say that's not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am here under oath and I can only tell the truth. I said what you have asked me and I have nothing else to add to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay, I'll move on. Now the document I did want you to look at was P-169, and I apologise to the Registrar for that. I had asked you some questions a moment ago about the role or the lack of role by the war presidency in the investigative body and then I wanted to show you this document. Perhaps the English version can be put on the overhead projector. Doctor, do you notice that at the top of this particular document, it's headed, "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Municipality of Konjic, War Presidency of the Municipality of Konjic, Investigative Body of the War Presidency"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have seen this document in its entirety. It has been shown to me and I will tell you exactly what I think of it. I see it now for the first time. I have never seen it before in my life. This document, at the bottom has a seal, which is not a seal of the body of which I was a -- the president. And it completely excludes the war presidency and any of its body in terms of the authorship. And as far as the heading of the document is concerned, you should ask the person who drafted it why he put it there. Any document that was coming out of the war presidency had to have a seal affixed to it and this is not the right seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. Now, if -- tell us about seals, Doctor. If a seal appears on something and a signature above it, does one give high regard to the seal or to the signature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The witness is complaining about the right seal, not necessarily any seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, he may be, Your Honour. This is operating, I might ask him about position in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is it the seal that determines the issue if there's any question of doubt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely. If there is no seal -- and only the war presidency had the seal. And if there is any other seal, he was made somewhere else. This document was not drafted in the war presidency or in any of its bodies and this is what I affirm, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Certainly. So if there was -- I just want to clarify this point. So if there was any confusion by -- in determining the competency of the person who appeared to sign a document, that confusion would be resolved by reference to the seal itself? Am I right in saying that? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That is what you have stated, that is not what I wanted to say. I said everything that I had to say on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, are you prepared to help us with this, Doctor, because you know more about what operated in Konjic Municipality at that relevant time than we did and I am asking you about the effective seals of various bodies -- let me finish, Doctor -- the effective seals by various bodies in the municipality, in that particular period of time. And the question that I am asking you is, if there is confusion, can that confusion be resolved by looking at the particular seal that's attached?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness has already stated, specifically, the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are talking about different seals. There was no other seal at the war presidency in Konjic. There was only one single seal. Any document coming out of the war presidency or any of its organs, would have to have had the war presidency seal affixed to it. And this is not such a seal. So I say that this document was not drafted, was not compiled in any -- in the war presidency or any of its organs and I think that this makes it entirely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can I have, Madam Registrar, Exhibits P-210 and P-213? Just to look at and then I want to show them to the witness. Just look at these two documents that I now show to you. And the matter that interests me most is the seals that are placed at the bottom of them. And when you've had a good look at them, would you put them on the ELMO for me, please. On this occasion, could we have the original document on the ELMO. Once the Doctor has looked at them. Okay. Can they be put on the ELMO, please? Original version, just one at a time. That's fine. Leave that one there for a moment until it comes up on the screen. Doctor, do you notice there appears two signatures there? One appears to be a document signed Zejnil Delalic and it's headed, "Coordinator". And the signature that immediately appears, appears to be signed by the TO commander, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I explained that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, just bear with me, Doctor. And you see that there are two seals attached, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, am I right in saying that both of those seals are the seals of the Konjic Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is beyond question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I object, I don't know if these are authentic documents and I don't know how this witness can pronounce his opinion about these documents because his signature is not on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the -- that they are two seals that you recognise as being the seals of the Konjic Territorial Defence and they are attached next to each of the signatures?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He's only been asked to identify these seals, which he can do if he knows what those seals were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see what bearing this has. Given the knowledge of this witness, he's president of the municipality and not of the TO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He can say he's not aware of those seals, he can say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In fact, he said, "absolutely", I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And just looking at the next document that I have given you, which is a similar document, and only reference to the seals again. Now I only want to see the seals on the second page. Now, again, there's two seals there, they're the seals of the Territorial Defence, are they not, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And there are two names that appear beside them. Now, does that mean that if Zejnil Delalic, for example, was to sign his name and attach a seal next to it, that if there was any confusion about his role or competency, we would resolve that confusion by reference to that seal that appears there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not agree, I will explain this to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here on this document, the signature, if this is actually the signature of Mr. Delalic, above that you have the word "coordinator". This is not the only document signed by him. And it is not a sign of the fact that this person is a military person, but, merely of a sign of his presence and of his information. We were aware of his status at that time and what he was at that time. And the document was written in a competent military body, which was confirmed by the seals and the coordinator, coordinator was only confirms that he was present at the time, so he was civilian then and he only transmitted information between the joint command and the war presidency and I don't see anything strange in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So that seal --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He's not a soldier in signing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So the seals really didn't mean very much at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not commenting on this. We know what his function was and what his signature means. We have clarified his post of coordinator on a number of occasions already, very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, yesterday, when you were speaking of the fact that the TO commanders would sign certain documents, and you signed documents with them as the war -- as president of the war presidency, it wouldn't matter where you put your seal or the TO's seal on the document next to your signature, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the documents, which the joint command sent to the war presidency had the character of a piece of information and vice versa. All documents of the war presidency sent to the joint command had the character of an information and not of an order. We could not order anything to the joint command and the joint command couldn't issue orders to us because we were quite different bodies, but we could issue to one another some piece of information related to an individual problem. So the war presidency could issue decisions only to management bodies or to the institutions established by it, like the civilian defence and so on, but not to any other military body.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, yesterday in your evidence you spoke of the fact that the war presidency formed a medical commission to examine persons and to provide medical care.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The war presidency, not the military presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do apologise, the war presidency, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And that medical commission also had responsibility for people in Celebici, as well as other persons in Konjic Municipality, that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the basis of this question of our colleague, it was not a question of the war presidency forming commission, it was the health centre that established commissions for medical examinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We'll check up on the transcripts, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But the health commission, in any event, came under the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Change the substance of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It doesn't change the substance, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The medical commission was formed by the health institution and the health institution was established by the municipalities, so the hospital in Konjic was under the competency of the municipality and this was all under the competencies of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So the health centre was in charge of taking care of the health of all the population of Konjic and to provide medical care to all of them. And I would like to avail myself of this opportunity to say that they did their utmost as colleagues and as health workers and medical personnel and doctors, regardless of who was in questions, they invested super human efforts because the times were very difficult indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What programme was in place on an ongoing basis to attend to the health needs of the prisoners of Celebici by this medical commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The health centre was very busy indeed. And it had obligations to the entire population of Konjic, so the prisoners, the detainees were in such a position that health could be provided to them in the same way as to the other population when such assistance was needed. The doctors and the staff provided such aid whenever this was necessary and that is a certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I am being just shown the transcript of what you actually said yesterday at 1004029 -- .29. And you say in answer to a question, after these police and military operations in these areas mentioned, the war presidency at its session, held on June 3rd of that year, adopted a series of conclusions, it mentions several events --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said June the 3rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you participated, did you not, as part of this medical commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a Doctor and there were very few doctors in the municipality. All the Serb physicians had left. And there was a shortage of medical persons. We even suggested to mobilise to include medical students, those who had not yet graduated, in our job. Anyone who had any sort of medical knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's not necessary, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, in most instances, the questions I ask you merely require a yes or no answer. Now, I don't want to restrict you if you think you need to explain something, but in most instances, you can satisfy my requirements by -- just wait please, Doctor -- you can satisfy my requirements by yes or no answer and we can resolve this much more quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I took part in examining in this board commission as a Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you examined people in Celebici as well, didn't you, you, yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, once.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, those people were brought to you, were they, it wasn't a case of you going out and making any determinations on your own, it was people that were actually brought to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We examined them in the compound of Celebici in the administrative building, that is, all people requiring examination. They were brought by the medical technicians to the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I was just endeavouring to clarify whether you had any input into the determination of who would receive or who wouldn't receive medical attention. Now, I think you also said in your evidence, and it's your position, I believe, that the injuries that you examined were not the result of someone being beaten but were more the results or consequences of war injuries. That's your position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that because people who are brought were brought following military and combat action and then we examined them. I took part in those examinations and the people were brought to us after the combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any of the prisoners that were actually taken away from Celebici for medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember the details. I think that I knew some of them. I knew a man called Mrkajic; that was his surname, and I think I remember a man called Jovanovic; that was his surname. I cannot be 100 per cent sure but I think that I can remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about a name called Slobodan Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Doesn't mean a thing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Zelko Klimenta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zelko Klimenta, I knew him but I hadn't seen him. I don't remember having had examined him, but I knew him from earlier. I don't remember that he was checked up by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were the medical records of the detainees of Celebici that you examined, kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were records kept by the medical technicians. This was not the job of a doctor, that is, writing in the names and surnames of the patients and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These medical technicians accompanied you to Celebici, did they, when you did your examinations so that these were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The entire job relating to examination was carried out by the health centre, that civilian institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you actually write on the medical records, sign them or make any note on them yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't really remember the details, but some diagnosis had to be written out. If people were more seriously injured, they were sent to hospital. And then there, there should have been documents about such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But are you saying there were no documents in relation to people actually examined at Celebici, only those that went to hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not what I'm claiming.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not trying to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But really what I'm asking you, Doctor, is are you aware that medical records were kept of the Celebici detainees examined at Celebici. That's what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a book probably. There must have been a book with the names of the persons coming to be examined were noted down. This is quite normal. This is the protocol of medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where would that book be now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know where it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, who determined which patients you would see and which ones you wouldn't see; do you know? It may be something you don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Did you examine all or some of them only? Did you examine all the detainees or only some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The detainees requiring medical assistance were provided with such medical assistance so whoever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Did you examine all the detainees or only those who required attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were no regular systematic check-ups, only those wishing to be examined or having any health problems were examined. I think that this is clear. I think that is the usual practise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You attended the camp, I think you said, on one occasion, in your capacity as a medical practitioner. Did you attend in any other capacity? Do you remember going out there for any other reason?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has said that on the oath taking ceremony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say that I visited the prison. I said that I had visited the compound of the Celebici, the barracks. I never went to the prison. I was in the administration building where I examined people on one occasion. On a second occasion, I went to the compound when there was the swearing-in ceremony, and I was in the official stalls there, in the solemn stalls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there any other doctors with you at the time you went to the camp to perform your medical duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was with you then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember there was Dr. Ahmed Izetbegovic (sic) who is a specialist of internal medicine.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The name is Jusufbegovic, sorry, Ahmed Jusufbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In the transcript it's "Izetbegovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, do you remember going to Celebici on one occasion at least when you spoke to Jasmin Guska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. On one occasion in those two cases I mentioned when we were examining patients, I saw Jasmin Guska in the circle. I didn't speak with him at all. I remember that I saw a colleague, a doctor, and I had a short talk with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember being at the camp and seeing Dr. Petko Grubac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not in the camp. I told you where I was. But a moment ago, I just said that I saw a colleague of mine who was a physician and this was Dr. Petko Grubac. I said that I saw him while I was going to the administration building because he was there and I had a very brief conversation with him. I recall very well that I told him on that occasion that I was not competent -- that I had nothing to do with his investigation, that he was a physician, that he was probably going to be treated quite humanely. I have nothing more to add to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see Jasmin Guska remove his glasses or force him to throw his glasses on the floor and then smash them. Did you witness that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know absolutely nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember ever attending a meeting in Zejnil Delalic's house, and specifically, the date I have is the 11th of July, 1992, when there was discussion about a military matter of setting up an ambush?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hear this for the first time indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you know nothing about that. Do you know a person or persons called Strahinja Sekic and Slobodan Draganic; do you know either of those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember ever receiving a call from people in a Serb village in the municipality, I shouldn't say a Serb village, but in a village in the municipality appealing to you to have grenade attacks stopped on the village; do you ever recall anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It's really too much to ask of me right now. There were so many things there. I really do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did people actually call you about military matters from time to time that you can recall, such as preventing firing on a village and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be honest with you, in my office, people work 24 hours a day, hundreds and hundreds of people pass through it. It's not something that I can really answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you think of Esad Ramic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: As what, as a commander, as a person or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As commander, as a person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. What is the meaning of that question? I don't understand. I know that he was the municipal headquarters commander, and as far as his personal qualities are concerned, I really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You had no complaints against him?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You had no complaints against him? That's all he can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I won't ask any more, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you give a statement on the 20th of June, 1993 at Pazavici to the 43rd Mountain Brigade of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really do not see any relevance to any of these questions and I object to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If my colleague is patient, Your Honours, all will be revealed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'd ask you to look at this document that I now show you. There's an English version and a Bosniak version, and there's a copy for Your Honours and a copy for the Defence, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution document 242.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, does your signature appear at the foot of each page of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember actually giving this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I need to object again. Again, this is a document drafted by a security body which, according to our law, can never be used in a court of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, their law has no application here, and I'm only dealing with one paragraph. I'll be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you intending to impeach his statement in any respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In some respects, yes, Your Honour, but only in one paragraph. It's a very short paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If that is not the case, I don't think it will be necessary to refer to it. What was it that he said you wanted to impeach?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I just want him to go, Your Honours, to the second -- I'll give it to him in his own language. In Your Honours' English version, the relevant paragraph to which I wish to take you is on the third page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What I'm asking is what do you intend to impeach? If it is not intended for that, then I don't think it will even be necessary to refer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, to explain the subject matter, I have to take Your Honour to the relevant part, and once I do, I can explain the subject matter much more easily, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think I don't like it that way, because if it will not be necessary to introduce it, the reading of that paragraph will not be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it goes to the question just a few moments ago about his opinion of Esad Ramic, and it goes to the question of his authorities and capacities to a point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's hear what he said here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Tell me what you're referring to the paragraph. "Zejnil set up a headquarters in his house. Zejnil and Esad did not like each other. As for" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to Judge Jan, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That's exactly right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: "He's an asshole. I would never have appointed him commander. That's what Zejnil told him so." How is it relevant? It doesn't show that Zejnil became the commander of the TO. It doesn't show he was responsible for setting up the Celebici camp. Why are you bringing documents which have no bearing on this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, with respect, the credibility of a witness is something that is very crucial and central, and he has already testified that he had no problems with Esad Ramic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He may not have problems, but the feeling of his professional competence is a different thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm not asking him about his professional competence. I'm asking him about his opinion of somebody, and he has already given me an answer and this would appear to contradict it. Your Honours, that's a standard approach of cross-examination and it deals with the issue of credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think there are differences of opinion expressed in other places and is relevant in the case, but I don't know what that matters to Delalic himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm not going to pursue it, Your Honours, but I note that I have attempted to deal with this issue in what I submit, with great respect, is a legitimate method of cross-examination, but anyway, I'll pass on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, in your evidence yesterday, you spoke of the fact that you did, on occasion, wear military uniforms but that was for official purposes; is that a fair summary of your evidence on that matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could also the microphone be put to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly check his microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, you tell me what you did say. Let's make sure we have this clear. What is your position? Why did you wear military uniforms in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That year many persons wore uniforms. I was a civilian organ, but it was an honour for me to wear a uniform. It was easier for me to work, to move around. It does not prove that I was a soldier. A number of people did this. This was the beginning of the war. It was something that was a matter of pride and honour. I see nothing bad in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you performed medical duties, so you're a man of medicine. You were the president of the war presidency and a civilian, but you occasionally wore military uniforms for limited purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I certainly did not wear it when I was in the surgery room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why did you carry a machine gun?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ask him did he carry a machine gun?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Actually, did you carry a machine gun?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the relevance of this. This is collateral to anything that has to do with the guilt of any of these defendants.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you carry a machine gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not an automatic rifle but I had my personal weapons. These were wartimes. There's nothing strange about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with weapons, Doctor, so you would need to forgive me, but is a Heckler, H-E-C-K-L-E-R, a small machine gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're asking me too much. I had a pistol. It was my personal weapon, if you really want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And that was what you wore on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the hospital, only when I would go to places where it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In the hospital, you carried a knife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a surgical knife, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I don't know whether the booth is ready to play a very small excerpt of Exhibit 109 which I have requested --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you think it's necessary to play that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, it goes to credibility. It's a video showing this gentleman, we will submit, at the appropriate time and we submit he's carrying a gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You talked about this particular type of gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is what the video will reveal, Your Honour, because they tend to be the most accurate form of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What he carried was a machine gun?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to engage in what is machine guns and what aren't, but it's more than a pistol, put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to this. It's irrelevant and collateral impeachment. It doesn't go to the heart of the issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I also would like to join in this objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There could always be danger of his being attacked. So if he carried a weapon, what is there to say about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A man of medicine, Your Honours and

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: And also a political leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I won't press it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If people that were in senior and responsible positions in the Konjic municipality, during that period, stated that they were members of the war presidency, I'm referring directly to the accused Mr. Delalic -- I'll withdraw that, Your Honours. Did the war presidency have any obligations to ensure that the Celebici detainees had adequate care, blankets and food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The war presidency, within the sphere of its own responsibilities, as well as the institutions that were subordinate to it, like the civilian protection agency and health care, needed to provide care for everyone including the prisoners. This was done through the civilian protection. This was done through collections. We did not have supplies of blankets and similar supplies. It was something that was a normal, regular activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you ultimately responsible to ensure that they received those sorts of needs and requirements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was very clear. The presidency had no responsibility over the prison, but the civilian bodies of the presidency, such as the civilian protection and an institution which was established by the presidency which was the hospital, did have such responsibility to collect the supplies such as blankets, medication. These medications would then be provided to the appropriate bodies who had responsibility for the prisoners. I think that is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is that all you have for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any re-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Several questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzihuseinovic, during the

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: certain decisions and orders. Can you tell me, Mr. Hadzihuseinovic, whether the war presidency in its role as the assembly was authorised to issue orders and decisions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, certainly it did have such authorities but only with respect to the civilian administration bodies and institutions that it had established such as the hospital, but in no way with respect to the military bodies, and this is what is stated in the statute of the town of Konjic in article 66.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you. You have spoken about that already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He explained it during cross-examination. He explained it properly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that this was also stated yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Hadzihuseinovic, just the issues that were not made absolutely clear. Now, I would like to show a couple of exhibits shown to you by the Prosecution, that is 5A-11, 5A/12. It's "/13." This is all part of D-144. Number 12 was not shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 5A/12 and 5A/13 were shown to the witness, so please, Counsel, be precise which document we should show?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please show two documents, 5A/12 and 5A/13?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What are these documents supposed to show?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: One is an order of 3 June regarding blankets, and the other one is the decision on the health centre. Those were the documents shown to the witness by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: You have both of the documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzihuseinovic, regarding the delivery, could you tell me whether the order was delivered to the command and to the logistics office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as an information.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the decision also delivered both to the command and to the logistics body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and also as an information.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Hadzihuseinovic. Is it true then that depending on who was to be informed, both decisions and orders were delivered in the same manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: I believe that we have now clarified a point that had not been made clear previously. There is another issue that needs to be clarified. Now that you have this decision regarding the health centre in front of you, is this the decision whereby the health centre is committing to providing certain health care to the detainees at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Is this the decision that you had referred to during your examination-in-chief and when you were shown part of the transcript by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: The medical commission, of which you were a part, and which was established by the health centre, was this a second commission which went there, immediately following the combat operations, to examine the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Hadzihuseinovic, and chairman of the municipal authority. We are very grateful for your assistance to the Tribunal. We appreciated your testimony. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The witness is discharged. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, you can bring your next witness at 12? The Trial Chamber will now rise and reassemble at 12 noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Would counsel be fairly nice to the -- to let us have an idea of what is being inflated on us again, whether it is a repetition of what has been going on or something different? Because I think we have had enough of some many stories of the same kind. So let's know where we are being led to this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this witness is the director of the war hospital. You will recall that certain prosecution witnesses mentioned him. And given the evidence that was provided, this will determine my leading of this witness. This is -- this most of all concerns the exculpatory evidence concerning the doctors. There may be some additional questions which would just give additional information. But, as I said yesterday, I will only limit myself to two or three areas that are crucial for our Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed. If we find that certain portions are getting announced again and again, we reserve the right not to let them in as evidence, but you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I call Mr. Ahmed Jusufbegovic. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you please swear the witness. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly take your seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, will you please state your name for the court, by giving us your full first and last names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My first is Ahmed Jusufbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufbegovic, will you please tell the court where and when were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Repovci, 1937, on March 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In order to make it very specific, could you please tell us where Repovci is located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Repovci is about 20 kilometres out of Konjic and the road from Konjic to Repovci passes through Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I think that clarifies it sufficiently. Mr. Jusufbegovic, can you tell me what your profession is and where were you educated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a physician, a specialist for internal medicine and my subspecialisation is in cardiology. My entire education was in Sarajevo. I graduated from the classical high school in Sarajevo and also the medical school. For a while I studied in Belgrade. I specialised in internal medicine in Sarajevo. Then I also went to graduate school and specialising in cardiology, also in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jusufbegovic, where were you and what was your position in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Konjic and I was on duty of the director of health centre in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufbegovic, the court is aware of a number of facts regarding the blockade of the town, so I am not here to dwell on these questions, being citizens who live there. My only question to you is, as a director of the health centre there, did you have certain problems in providing health care and transportation of your patients during this period and what were the reasons, if so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. During that period, in the institution where I worked, which was the health centre, the problems we were facing were very complex. We were a health centre, which was not adequately supplied with medication, medical supplies and other equipment and machinery, which was necessary to provide medical care to the regular patients and the new ones, which were now -- which now appeared because of the war. In other words, we had lack of just about everything we needed for our work.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufbegovic, where were you taking more serious patients, that is, patients with more serious conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war broke out, we were transferring all our patients who needed serious medical care to Mostar or Sarajevo. However, in late April, all roads were blocked and no patient could leave Konjic any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more general question, Mr. Jusufbegovic, did you have any personal experiences in your attempts to send these seriously ill patients out of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My personal experiences related to some time around 1 May 1992. We had chemo-dialysis in Sarajevo. And there were six patients whose lives depended on this chemo-dialysis and I personally took them into ambulances to Sarajevo. At the village of Bradina, there was a check point where we were stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Doctor, do you know Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you were close friends?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can this friendship influence your testimony? In other words, can you speak the full and whole truth, regardless of this fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have given a solemn declaration that I would be speaking truth and nothing but the truth and I will abide by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a friend of Mr. Zejnil Delalic, do you know whether Mr. Zejnil Delalic, before the war or during the war, was a member of any political party in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Zejnil Delalic did not belong to any party.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was a member of any government body in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not a member of any government body in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufbegovic, do you know whether Mr. Zejnil Delalic, in the period before he became the commander of a tactical group, did take part in any combat operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only know that he took part as a civilian in transportation of material from the Celebici barracks to the Ovcara farm, which was the property of his sister's.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jusufbegovic, were (redacted) (redacted) Dr. Petko Grubac persons whom you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these are my long time colleagues. They both worked in the same organisation where I worked, and together with Dr. Grubac, I went to school.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufbegovic, do you know whether these physicians, at some point in 1992, left your institution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In late April, I believe, I think it was around 20th of April, they left our institution, our organisation, and moved to Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Jusufbegovic, do you know whether there were any military activities conducted in Konjic in order to lift the blockade of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were such activities in order to lift a blockade of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Jusufbegovic, do you know that in the course of these combat operations, (redacted) Dr. Grubac were captured and detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Jusufbegovic, how did you find out and from whom (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found that out from Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe this to us briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Some time before dawn, I received a call from Mr. Delalic. That was -- that night was very busy. I don't know exactly how many wounded we received that night, but we did work through the night. I had just left to take a rest when the physician on duty called me and told me that Mr. Delalic was on the telephone asking for me. And we talked and (redacted) with him and that he would send him. If I accepted, because he requested it, because he was on my staff, that he was slightly injured and that he needed certain medical help. And he also suggested in this conversation that it would be good since I was already deficient in medical staff, that we should keep the doctor so that he would continue to work at the hospital. I accepted this request and I agreed that (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Jusufbegovic, regarding this conversation, can you perhaps recall whether Mr. Zejnil Delalic told you who else was present there and whether this other person is also requesting this favour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that Dinko Zebic had brought

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have now twice stated that you were asked by Mr. Zejnil Delalic to do this, can you tell me now whether Mr. Zejnil Delalic issued you an order or could he have issued you an order to do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no order issued. Zejnil Delalic was no superior of mine. My organisation, that is where I was the director, was reporting to its founder and this was the municipal assembly. And at this time, the war presidency had already been established, so I only could have received an order from the war presidency and its president.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufbegovic,(redacted) (redacted) did you fulfil the request of Mr. Zejnil Delalic and Mr. Dinko Zebic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, before you go on, since you said that there were a lot of wounded and injured and you worked the whole day and night, can you tell me when this all took place -- or, let me be very specific, was this during the operations at Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly at that time. I believe that the Bradina operation was not quite finished yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, now please go on, what happened

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The staff was not in a great mood. The rumours started going around that the doctor who had left us, who was detained at Bradina is now supposed to be working with us. And there are wounded persons, people who were maimed who were coming from that same area and it would be kind of awkward for me now to accept him as a staff member.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted) a while as a patient and what happened with him next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I justified his stay there because he was a patient. He was lightly injured and I wanted to sort of pacify the staff and I received him in the gynaecological ward, where I believe he stayed for two nights.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Jusufbegovic, did you later on learn, or did you learn at all, that Dr. Petko Grubac was also captured and detained at Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As the director of the health centre, was it part of your responsibility to immediately respond and provide medical care to persons who were injured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. We provided first aid to any person who was injured, regardless of who they were. My institution never discriminated between any -- between any kind of -- different patients or injured, regardless of who they were. We only prioritise by the degree of emergency.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you said that there was a lot of work during those couple of days, did you learn whether there were injured persons among those who were offering resistance to the defence forces in those operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were injured.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As director of the health centre and as a physician, did you do what was necessary in order to examine these injured persons? And if you did, can you tell us what it was that you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We immediately established a commission, which was tasked with examining all the injured, to provide medical care, the first aid; for those who needed additional medical care, those persons were to be transferred to the hospital where they could be provided such care. And members of this commission included a surgeon, Rusmir Hadzihuseinovic, then it was Dr. Hajduk and myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you conduct the examination of these detained persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The examination was conducted in an administration building at Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were the examined persons provided adequate medical care at that time, that is a kind of medical care that your health centre was able to provide at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did provide adequate care to all persons who were in need of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, now let us switch over to another topic. Tell me, in the course of 1992, in any point of time, were you ever engaged in liberating your colleagues, (redacted) and Dr. Grubac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe to us or tell us how this took place, at whose request, and tell us everything you know about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this happened at the end of July, and it was the second half of July, actually. One evening in my surgery, I was -- I had a telephone call from Mr. Delalic and he told me that on that day, Grubac Gordana had visited him that day, who is the wife of Dr. Grubac. Perhaps she asked for me, but she couldn't find me for some reason and he was very surprised that those persons were still being detained and that something should be done as -- being friends of those doctors, he was their friend and I was even in family relations with Dr. Grubac because we were, in fact, witnesses at our marriages. And that -- and then I tried to meet that request as quickly and as fast as I could, as quickly as possible. We'd agreed that on the following morning, Mr. Delalic should come to me and that we should make use of all our friends and connections because I must say, publicly, in front of this court, that friendly relations are very much in fashion even today and that is how business is usually concluded. And our agreement was, in fact, being implemented the following morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Jusufbegovic, the next morning, did Mr. Delalic, in accordance with that agreement, come to you, and what did you do on that day to help Dr. Grubac 5, (redacted) helping them to be released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic came with his driver and I said to him, "I will go to 100 doors, knock at 100 doors in Konjic to see what can be done and to do everything I can to have these doctors released." Mr. Delalic remained in hospital, because it was a general war hospital, to see some of the wounded. I went to the civilian protection unit, to the military investigative commission, and all the people that I believed to be willing to help, I looked for such people. Unfortunately, I was not able to conclude this business because these people could not give me the records which could make it possible for these people to leave the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Delalic on that day again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We met again and I told him, I told Zejnil, that I was not able to finish the business as we had thought we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you then and from whom find out that Zejnil Delalic was in a certain way a party to the signing of a document for the release of a certain person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Zejnil remembered a few days before, that on the basis of a consent of one of the commanders, he signed the release sheet in the military investigative command or in the Territorial Defence. Then his driver went off, and after an hour or so, he brought us those two papers, those discharge sheets from the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, on that day, did you talk to anyone else about the release of those doctors in addition to Mr. Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke to a number of people, but the key person who was able to help was the commander. I told him, since I have these papers with me, I have to find Esad Ramic who was commander at the time and that I would ask him for this because I'm responsible for those doctors, and I could not really figure out or understand that they had been in a conspiracy or that they had done anything bad. I really wished to see them released and that I would continue to be responsible for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before I ask you the following question, could you tell me when you heard that they had been detained, did you hear from anyone why these doctors were being detained, the reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
